The world is a dangerous place

issues.explanation: For stalking trauma, 'Betrayal' can be plausible if the stalker was known to the patient, but the profile provides no supporting items suggesting an interpersonal betrayal context. More importantly, 'Contamination' is typically associated with sexual assault or physical violation and is hard to reconcile clinically with stalking in the absence of any other items indicating assault, bodily intrusion, or abuse.

Within Negative Appraisals, 'Betrayal' and 'Contamination' point to different trauma meanings: interpersonal trust violation versus bodily violation. They can coexist in some cases, but with stalking alone and no corroborating memory, trigger, or threat items, this combination is clinically difficult to justify.

For stalking trauma, 'I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened' is hard to reconcile unless there was an additional sexual or physical assault element. On its face, this appraisal is clinically incongruent with the stated trauma type.

'Avoid Medical Care' implies avoidance centered on trauma-related examination, disclosure, or bodily injury/assault concerns, but there are no Memory, Threat, or Trigger items indicating injury, assault, or medical trauma. It is poorly matched to the rest of this stalking profile.

vignette:
Aroha Tane is a twenty-year-old auditor of Māori and Pacific Islander descent who was referred for psychological assessment following a prolonged stalking ordeal that began eighteen months ago and left her, in her own words, "a completely different person." Her PCL-5 score of 64 places her firmly in the severe range, and the clinical picture that has emerged across intake and early sessions is one of a young woman whose sense of safety, identity, and future have all collapsed inward around a single, sustained threat.

The stalking began during Aroha's first year at the accounting firm where she still works. A former acquaintance - someone she had known briefly through a shared social circle - began appearing outside her office building, sending messages through colleagues, and leaving items at her workstation. For several months, Aroha had no formal language for what was happening; she only knew that she could not predict when he would appear, that the boundary between her professional life and her personal safety had dissolved entirely, and that nowhere felt closed off to him. The ordeal ended only after a restraining order was obtained, but by then the damage to her internal world was profound. The office building where she had once felt competent and purposeful had become, in her nervous system, a site of exposure. Even now, arriving at work each morning, scanning the lobby before stepping through the door, she feels the same low-grade dread she felt during the worst months - her eyes moving to faces, exits, anyone standing still too long.

That hypervigilance is not experienced by Aroha as a symptom but as rational necessity. She has come to believe, with a certainty that feels unshakeable, that the world is genuinely dangerous and that her continued safety depends entirely on her own alertness. This conviction that the world is an unsafe place, and that her life has been fundamentally and perhaps irreparably destroyed by what happened, has shaped the strategies she now uses to manage daily life in ways that have quietly narrowed it to almost nothing. Because she is certain the threat is ongoing - not necessarily from him, but from the world as it now presents itself to her - she has stopped going out beyond what is absolutely required. Weekends pass inside her apartment. Invitations from colleagues are declined. The few friendships she had when she started the job have thinned to almost nothing, partly because she no longer appears, and partly because she no longer tries. Her appraisal that her life has been destroyed makes any effort to rebuild it feel not just futile but somehow dishonest - as though reaching for something good would be a kind of lie about what she is now.

This is where the picture becomes most painful. Aroha does not simply avoid danger; she avoids anything that might make her feel hopeful. A colleague's birthday lunch, a message from an old friend, a film she might once have enjoyed - these are things she turns away from, not because they frighten her in the way a stranger's gaze does, but because she has come to believe she does not deserve them. She tells herself, quietly and with a kind of bleak consistency, that she deserves to suffer for what happened - as though the stalking were something she had invited or failed to prevent, and as though happiness now would be a form of cheating some just sentence. These patterns of self-punishment and withdrawal did not arrive all at once; they accumulated over months, each small refusal reinforcing the belief that preceded it, each belief making the next refusal feel more reasonable. The result is a young woman who goes to work, performs her auditing duties with technical competence, returns home, and otherwise inhabits a life that has been stripped of almost everything that once gave it texture.

What finally brought Aroha to seek help was a conversation with her supervisor, who gently noted that she had not taken a single day of leave in a year and that she looked, in his words, exhausted in a way that sleep did not seem to fix. She came to the first session saying very little about what she hoped for, and a great deal about what she feared - specifically, that she had already become the person the stalking made her, and that there was no version of herself left on the other side of it.
